q: You are running down the trades at 20°N and want a dawn star fix. When do you have both the stars and a usable horizon?
o: From 0630 LMT, once the Sun is up
why: Between nautical twilight (Sun 12° down: the horizon appears) and civil twilight (6° down: the stars fade) you have both.

q: You are on the ARC route at 16°N, planning the evening stars. What time do you take for the end of civil twilight?
why: Interpolate between the rows: 16°N is 0.6 of the way from 10°N to 20°N; 1800 − 0.6 × 16 min = 1750 LMT.

q: You have sailed from the Channel down to 10°N. What does this almanac extract mean for your evening star sights?
a: The window is shorter — be on deck and ready early
o: The window is longer — there is no need to hurry
The window is the same — only the clock changes
Stars can be taken only after nautical twilight here
why: In low latitudes the Sun sinks steeply: civil to nautical twilight takes 24 min at 10°N against 38 min at 50°N.

q: Your crew wants one more star before supper. What do you tell them?
a: Stop — the horizon is too dim to trust
o: Go on — the stars are at their brightest now
Go on, with a darker shade on the telescope
Go on, and add 5′ for the dim horizon
why: After nautical twilight the horizon fades; an altitude measured to a blurred horizon can put the line miles out.

fig.title: Dusk, 20 Jan, lat 14°N
lines: Now 1849: the horizon is a grey blur

q: You are 600 miles west of the Cape Verdes at dusk with time for three stars before the horizon goes. Which three do you take?
why: Altitudes 20°–70°, azimuths about 120° apart: 073°, 168°, 330°. Peacock is too low; the other sets lie within 180°.

q: Your star finder offers six stars, all between 25° and 60° high. Which three azimuths give you the best three-star fix?
why: Three lines cut best with the bodies about 120° apart; reciprocal bearings give parallel lines, a narrow fan gives shallow cuts.

q: Bound for St Helena, you have planned these four stars for the evening fix. In what order do you shoot them?
why: At dusk the brightest stars show first while the horizon is still sharp: take Sirius first and leave fainter Aldebaran for last.

q: Before dawn you work out where Arcturus will be, so you can find it in the half-light. What do you preset on the sextant, and where do you look?
why: LHA = 217°09.0′ + 145°48′ − 52° = 310°57.0′; the formula gives Hc 43°28′, Zn 080°, east of you (LHA over 180°).

q: Before evening twilight you set up the star finder to see which stars will be up. Which two things do you set it for?
a: Your latitude and LHA Aries at twilight
o: Your longitude and the Sun's GHA
Your latitude and the Sun's declination
LHA Aries and the Moon's declination
why: Take the template for your latitude and set it to LHA Aries at twilight; it then shows each star's altitude and azimuth.

q: You want the star finder set for tonight's twilight on the Puddle Jump. Which LHA Aries do you set?
You plan tonight's stars with HO 249 Volume 1. What do you enter the table with?
o: Your latitude and each star's SHA
Your longitude and the time in UT
Each star's LHA and its Dec
why: Vol 1 is entered with Lat and LHA Aries: it lists seven selected stars with Hc and Zn, the best three for a fix marked ◆.

q: You have plotted a fix from Volume 1's selected stars. What must you still do to it?
a: Move it by the precession correction in Table 5
o: Apply the v and d corrections to each Hc
Correct each Hc by 1′ for every year
why: Precession slowly shifts the stars; Table 5 gives the small move of the fix for years either side of the tables' epoch.

fig.title: HO 249 Volume 1
lines: Fix plotted from three selected stars

q: Halfway from Bermuda to the Azores, the cloud clears for a moment and you shoot a bright star you cannot name. Which star was it?
why: sin Dec = sin Lat sin Ho + cos Lat cos Ho cos Zn: Dec N11°44′; LHA 43° (west), SHA = LHA − LHA Aries ≈ 207°.

q: On the trade-wind route at 24°N, an unknown star crosses your meridian due south. Which star is it?
why: z = 90° − 54°32′ = 35°28′; star bearing south: Dec = Lat − z = S11°18′. On the meridian LHA = 0, so SHA = 360° − 201°36′ = 158°24′.

q: At dusk a gap in the cloud shows a bright star you do not recognise, and you take its altitude. What else do you note to identify it afterwards?
a: The exact time and its compass bearing
o: Its colour and how much it twinkles
The Moon's bearing at the same moment
why: Altitude, azimuth and time give its Dec and SHA by formula or the star finder; then you find it in the almanac's star list.

q: Off the Leeward Islands, you reduce a dawn sight of Sirius from the DR. What is the star's LHA?
You have already worked LHA Aries for your AP and now want Regulus's LHA. What is it?
why: LHA★ = LHA Aries + SHA: 312°10.4′ + 207°36′ = 519°46.4′; take off 360°: 159°46.4′ (the star is west of you).

q: You are crossing the Indian Ocean from Chagos towards the Seychelles. What is Rigel's LHA?
why: Longitude east is added: 298°33.2′ + 72°14.5′ = 370°47.7′; take off 360°: LHA 10°47.7′.

q: Bound from Bermuda to the Azores, you reduce your evening sight of Vega from the DR. What intercept and azimuth do you plot?
On passage from Cape Town to St Helena, you reduce an evening sight of Canopus from the DR. What do you plot?
You compare your observed and calculated altitudes of Spica. What is the intercept?
why: Ho 37°02.6′ − Hc 36°55.9′ = 6.7′; Ho is greater, so the intercept is towards the star.

q: Bound from Tahiti for Rarotonga, at 23°S, you take Z from the tables for a star. What is its true azimuth Zn?
why: South latitude with LHA over 180°: Zn = 180° − Z = 180° − 094° = 086°.

q: You shot an unnamed star and want to identify it with the star finder. How do you use it?
why: Set the template to LHA Aries at the sight; the star is under Ho 52° and the true bearing, 105° − 2°W = 103°.

q: You will reduce a sight of Antares off the coast of Brazil with HO 249. Which assumed position do you use?
why: AP latitude: the nearest whole degree. AP longitude: the one nearest the DR that makes LHA whole: 251°36.8′ − 36°36.8′ = 215°.

q: You plot your Deneb sight from its assumed position. Where do you draw the position line?
a: At right angles to the azimuth, 6 M towards Deneb
o: Along the azimuth line, through the AP
At right angles to the azimuth, 6 M away from Deneb
At right angles to the azimuth, through the AP
why: Measure the intercept from the AP along the azimuth (towards the body), then draw the position line at right angles there.

q: All three of your stars lie in the eastern sky, and their lines give this cocked hat. What do you make of it?
a: You may be outside it — add a star in the west
o: You are at its centre — plot it and go on
You are at the corner nearest the DR
It is small, so the fix is good to a mile
why: With all the bodies on one side, a constant error moves every line the same way, so the true position can lie outside the triangle.

q: Four star lines give this plot: three meet in a point and the Spica line passes 8 miles off. What do you do?
a: Take the point where three meet; recheck Spica
o: Average all four and take the middle
Trust Spica — it was the brightest star
Discard the lot and wait for noon
why: Three lines agreeing in a point outweigh one; the odd line is likely the wrong star, a mistimed sight or a slip in the working.

q: You reduce three stars with HO 249, so each has its own assumed position with a different longitude. How do you plot them?
a: Plot each intercept from its own AP
o: Plot every intercept from the DR
Average the three APs and plot from that
Use the first star's AP for all three
why: Each intercept belongs to the AP it was worked from; plot each from its own AP and the lines cross at the fix.

q: Your Antares sight comes out 4.5′ away. How do you lay off the intercept?
a: Measure 4.5 M from the AP towards 321°
o: Measure 4.5 M from the AP towards 141°
Measure 4.5 M from the AP towards 051°
Measure 4.5 M from the AP towards 231°
why: Away: measure from the AP in the reciprocal of Zn, 141° + 180° = 321°, and draw the position line at right angles there.

q: You want the fix for 1911, the time of your last sight. What do you do with the Capella line?
why: 1854 to 1911 is 17 min at 7.5 kn = 2.1 M: transfer the Capella line 2.1 M along the course, 250°.

q: Instead of moving the Deneb line on the plot, you correct its intercept for the run to 1916. What intercept do you plot?
why: Run 24 min at 8 kn = 3.2 M; its part towards Deneb is 3.2 × cos 60° = 1.6 M; 3.4′ + 1.6′ = 5.0′ towards.

q: You reduce an evening sight of Venus taken at 1823:40 UT. What is its GHA?
why: 142°17.6′ + 5°55.0′ = 148°12.6′; v −0.9 for 24 min gives −0.4′: GHA 148°12.2′. Venus's v can be negative.

q: Working a sight of Mars taken at 2142:08 UT, you open the increments page. What is Mars's GHA?
why: Planets use the Sun/planets column: 77°31.4′ + 10°32.0′ + v 0.8′ (1.1 × 42/60) = 88°04.2′.

q: You want a fix this afternoon, not at dusk. What do you do?
a: Preset Venus's Hc and sweep along its Zn
o: Wait for dusk — planets cannot be seen by day
Take a second sun line five minutes later
Take the Sun's upper limb for a second line
why: Bright Venus can be found by day with the sextant preset to its Hc on its Zn; its line crosses the sun line for a fix.

fig.title: Afternoon, mid-Atlantic
lines: Venus mag −4.6, 45° east of the Sun
Clear sky; Venus's Hc and Zn worked out

q: Jupiter is the bright, steady light in the east at dusk, and you have shot it. Where do you find its GHA and Dec?
a: In its own column on the almanac's daily page
o: In the star list, from its SHA
From the Sun's GHA and declination
why: Planets move against the stars, so each has GHA and Dec hourly in its own daily-page column; only stars are worked from SHA.

q: Bound from Cocos Keeling to Rodrigues, you take Jupiter at dawn and work it from the DR. What intercept and azimuth do you plot?
At 0930 you want a Moon sight to cross with the Sun. Which limb do you bring down to the horizon?
a: The upper limb — the lit edge
o: The lower limb — it is always the lower
The centre — judge it by eye
The lower limb — the dark edge is sharper
why: Always use the lit limb, and the lit side faces the Sun: with the Sun higher than the Moon, the top edge is lit.

fig.title: Morning Moon
lines: Last-quarter Moon, low in the west
Sun well up in the east
The Moon's bright side faces up

q: You correct an upper-limb Moon sight with the almanac's Moon tables. What is Ho?
why: Ha + first part 54.1′ + second part, U column 1.7′ − 30′ for the upper limb = 41°43.8′.

q: Approaching Fernando de Noronha, you work your afternoon Moon sight from the DR. What intercept and azimuth do you plot?
You need Venus's declination for a sight at 1845 UT. What is it?
why: The next hour shows Dec increasing: d 0.9′ × 45/60 = 0.7′; S21°14.2′ + 0.7′ = S21°14.9′.

q: You take the Sun and the half Moon within minutes of each other in the afternoon. What do the two position lines give you?
a: They cut at about 74° — a good fix
o: They cut at about 16° — too fine to use
They run parallel — no fix by day
They cut at about 37° — latitude only
why: Lines cut at the angle between the azimuths: 238° − 132° = 106°, i.e. 74°. Near the quarters the Moon is about 90° from the Sun.

q: What is the Moon's GHA for your sight at 1531:20 UT?
Your GPS has failed mid-ocean and you want Sun–Moon fixes by day. Around which days of this month do you plan them?
a: Around the 16th and the 31st — the quarters
o: Any day the Moon is in the sky
why: Near the quarters the Moon is about 90° from the Sun and up by day; at new Moon it is lost in the glare, at full Moon up only at night.

q: One of your three dawn sights gives this. What do you do with it?
a: Leave it out — it was not Sirius
o: Plot it — the DR must be 128 miles out
Move the fix halfway towards its line
Rework the other two from its AP
why: A huge intercept and a bearing 40° off the prediction mean the wrong body; fix from the two good lines and a re-shot star.

fig.title: “Sirius”
lines: The other two stars agree within 1.5′

q: At dusk you look for Capella where you predicted it and see this. Which light do you bring down?
o: Whichever is easier to hold in the mirror
Neither — Capella cannot be up yet
why: Capella matches the predicted Hc and Zn and is about as bright as Vega; a brilliant steady light near it is a planet.

fig.title: Dusk, looking for Capella
lines: At 046°: a brilliant steady light, 28° up
At 043°: a star as bright as Vega, 31° up

q: Your star finder still has Jupiter marked where you plotted it a month ago. What do you do before tonight's planning?
a: Re-plot it from this week's almanac SHA and Dec
o: Nothing — a planet keeps its SHA like a star
Move it by the Table 5 precession correction
Leave it off — planets cannot go on a star finder
why: Planets wander among the stars; the almanac's daily pages give their current SHA and Dec to plot them afresh.

fig.title: Star finder, before twilight
lines: Venus and Mars not yet plotted

q: Cloud let you have only one star at dawn. You want a running fix at 0935 with your sun line. What do you do?
a: Advance the star line 21 M along 260°
o: Advance the star line 21 M along 080°
Advance the sun line 21 M along 260°
Advance the star line 6 M along 260°
why: 0605 to 0935 is 3h30m at 6 kn = 21 M: advance the earlier star line 21 M along 260° to cross the sun line.

q: Cloud is building and you may get only one star at dusk to cross with your advanced afternoon sun line. Which star do you take first?
why: Deneb's line cuts the sun line at about 91°; the others bear within 30° of the Sun's azimuth or its reciprocal.

fig.title: Sun line 1530, Zn 239°
lines: Dusk stars from the star finder:

q: You come on deck for dawn sights and the stars are still bright. What are you waiting for before the first sight?
a: The horizon to sharpen below the stars
o: The stars to grow brighter in the dark
The Sun's upper limb to show
The Moon to light up the horizon
why: At dawn the stars are there first and you wait for the horizon; at dusk the horizon is sharp and you wait for the stars.

q: At dawn you plan these four stars. In what order do you take them?
why: At dawn the faintest stars fade first: start with Dubhe and keep bright Arcturus for last, as the sky lightens.

q: A crew member on her first ocean passage asks which planets she can use for sights. Which four have their own columns in the almanac?
why: The almanac tabulates GHA and Dec for the four navigational planets: Venus, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn. Mercury keeps too close to the Sun.

q: Bound from Rio for Cape Town, you take Achernar at dusk and work it from the DR. What Hc and Zn do you get?
why: LHA = 335°27.5′ + 335°21′ − 22°40′ = 288°08.5′: west longitude is subtracted. The formula then gives Hc 35°23.9′, Zn 141°.

q: Bound from Shetland to Norway at midsummer, you want a star fix tonight. When do you take it?
a: Between 2314 and 0049 LMT, bright stars only
o: Between 2128 and 2314 LMT, in civil twilight
After nautical twilight ends, as usual
Not tonight — no star will show at all
why: The Sun never gets 12° down, so the horizon stays all night; between the two civil twilights only the brightest stars and planets show.

q: South of St Helena in July, you will have a noon latitude today. Which dawn star gives the best line to cross with it?
why: The noon Sun bears north, so its line runs east–west; Rigel at Zn 086° gives a north–south line that cuts it near 90°.

q: It is 0200 under a bright Moon and you doubt your DR. What is the catch if you take star sights now?
a: The bright horizon under the Moon may be false
o: Stars near the Moon need its parallax
The stars are too faint to find by moonlight
why: The Moon's glitter can show a line short of the true horizon: trust a moonlit horizon only when other lines confirm it.

fig.title: 0200, mid-ocean
lines: Full Moon 50° up in the south-west

q: Leaving Cape Town for Brazil, you plan the first dusk fix. Which three stars do you take?
why: The bright southern stars bunch in the south: take Canopus 137°, Fomalhaut 252° and Aldebaran 012°. Acrux and Peacock are low.

q: Bound from Sydney for Lord Howe Island at 33°S, you work Antares with HO 249. What is its true azimuth?
why: South latitude, LHA under 180° (the star is west of you): Zn = 180° + Z = 180° + 095° = 275°.

q: At dawn off the Marquesas the eastern horizon is sharp but the west is still dark and hazy. In what order do you take these four stars?
why: At dawn the eastern horizon sharpens first and the western last: start with Altair in the east and leave Spica, in the west, till last.

fig.title: Dawn, 15 Mar, 15°S 140°W
lines: Horizon: sharp in the east, hazy in the west

q: Crossing the Arabian Sea from Salalah towards Cochin, you take Fomalhaut at dusk and work it from the DR. What Hc and Zn do you get?
why: LHA = 252°58.7′ + 15°18′ + 60°18′ = 328°34.7′. Dec S with Lat N: contrary names, so Dec goes in negative: Hc 36°55.4′, Zn 145°.

q: On passage from the Faroes to Iceland in October, you plan the dusk fix at 62°N. Which three stars do you take?
why: High in the north many stars stand near the zenith: Deneb is 71° up. Arcturus, Altair and Mirfak are 20°–70° up and about 120° apart.

q: Hove-to in a gale in the Agulhas Current, you get two stars 39 minutes apart. How do you bring the first line up to the time of the second?
why: Hove-to, the boat still drifts: 39 min at 1.5 kn = 1.0 M. Move the first line 1.0 M along the drift, 225°.

fig.title: Hove-to off South Africa, dusk
lines: Drift from the last fixes: 225°, 1.5 kn

q: On your first night in the South Pacific, you want Acrux for the dusk fix. Where on the Southern Cross do you look?
a: At the foot — the bright star nearest the pole
o: At the head — the top of the long arm
At the east end of the cross-bar
In the middle, where the two arms meet
why: Acrux is the foot of the Cross; the long arm, from the head through Acrux, points towards the south celestial pole.

q: Leaving Fremantle for Mauritius, you will reduce Spica with HO 249. Which assumed position do you use?
why: East longitude is added: choose the minutes that make LHA whole, 287°23.6′ + 115°36.4′ = 403° = LHA 43°, and the latitude nearest the DR.

q: In the afternoon mid-Atlantic, you have a sun line and two other bodies in the sky. Which do you take to cross with the Sun?
a: The Moon — its line cuts the sun line at 85°
o: Venus — it is the brighter of the two
Venus — it is nearer the Sun in the sky
Neither — wait for the dusk stars
why: Lines cut at the difference in azimuth: Sun–Moon 85°, Sun–Venus 49°. The Moon, near first quarter, gives the better fix.

q: Crossing the trades, you shoot three stars over 32 minutes while the North Equatorial Current sets you west. How do you move the first line to the time of the last?
why: Advance by the run over the ground: 3.5 M along 255° plus 0.5 M along 280° = 4.0 M along 258°.

q: Bound for Tristan da Cunha, you look over tonight's planned stars. Which one do you leave out?
o: Achernar — it is too near the meridian
Peacock — it is too far south
why: At 87° the azimuth is hard to judge and the sextant hard to swing; keep to 20°–70° — Hamal at 21° still serves.

q: You plot three star intercepts from one AP. Which point is the fix?
why: Lay off 3.5′ towards 040°, 0.9′ away from 160° and 2.6′ away from 280°: the lines meet 3 M east and 2 M north of the AP.

q: You want the fix for 1910, the time of your middle star. What do you do with the Rigel line taken at 1920?
o: Leave it — it is the last sight
why: Retire it to 1910: 10 min at 7 kn = 1.2 M back along the track, 075°. The 1858 line goes 1.4 M forward along 255°.

q: Halfway along the ARC to St Lucia, you add Saturn to the dusk fix and work it from the DR. What do you plot?
Approaching the Virgin Islands, you want Venus in tonight's dusk fix. When do you take it?
a: First, at about 1800, while it is over 10° up
o: Last, at the end of nautical twilight
With the stars, once they all show
Never — a planet is too bright to use
why: Venus shows long before the stars and sinks fast: take it first, above 10°, before the large and uncertain refraction near the horizon.

q: The dusk sky is clear and you have time for five stars. A crew member says three is enough. Why take all five?
a: An odd line shows up and can be left out
o: Five lines always make the hat smaller
Each extra star halves the error of the fix
The almanac's corrections need five sights
why: With three lines a bad sight hides inside the hat; with four or five, the lines that agree show up the one that does not.

q: Venus is crossing the equator this morning. What declination do you use for your sight at 1145 UT?
why: Dec moves 1.2′ an hour northward: S0°00.7′ + 0.9′ north (45/60 of 1.2′) crosses the equator: N0°00.2′.

q: Your afternoon sun line, run up to dusk, passes 5 miles south of a neat three-star fix. What do you make of it?
a: Trust the stars — the 22 M run carries the error
o: Move the fix halfway to the sun line
Trust the sun line — the Sun is the surer body
Rework the stars — three lines cannot all be wrong
why: The stars were taken together, with no run; the sun line was carried 22 M on the log and compass, so any current or leeway sits in it.

fig.title: Dusk, 1840
lines: Sun line at 1500, run up 22 M (6 kn)
It passes 5 M south of the star fix

q: You will correct tonight's Moon sight. Where do you find the Moon's horizontal parallax?
a: On the daily page, beside its GHA and Dec for the hour
o: In the star list at the back of the almanac
In HO 249 Volume 1, with the selected stars
On the increments page, beside v and d
why: The Moon's HP changes through the month (about 54′ to 61′), so the daily page gives it hour by hour with GHA, v, Dec and d.

q: South of Madagascar, bound for Durban, you take the Moon at dusk and work it from the DR. What do you plot?
Working tonight's Moon sight, what declination do you take for 0438 UT?
why: The next hour shows Dec falling: d 9.5′ × 38/60 = 6.0′; N23°35.7′ − 6.0′ = N23°29.7′. The Moon's d is large: never skip it.

q: Mid-Atlantic at dusk, your Rigel sight comes out 87 miles away. What do you make of it?
a: You took Betelgeuse — rework it as Betelgeuse
o: The DR is 87 miles out — plot it
The horizon was poor — leave it out
Rework it as Rigel from a new AP
why: Its altitude and bearing fit Betelgeuse, Orion's other bright star, about 20° from Rigel: rework it with Betelgeuse's SHA and Dec.

q: Your mate's three-star plot gives a 7-mile cocked hat, and you find he plotted Altair's intercept the wrong way. How far does the Altair line move when you correct it?
why: The line lay 3.5 M on the wrong side of the AP; corrected, it moves 2 × 3.5 = 7.0 M towards Altair.

q: At dawn between the Azores and the Caribbean, you work Jupiter and Rigel from the same DR. Where is your fix?
why: Rigel away at 181°: 2.9′ north. Jupiter towards at 088°: 3.9 M east = 4.4′ of longitude at 28°N: 28°12.9′N 40°20.6′W.

q: Planning tonight's dusk fix, you read the almanac's planet notes for the month. Which planets can you add to your stars?
why: Only planets above the horizon at dusk help: Jupiter and Saturn. Venus rises before dawn and Mars is lost in the Sun's glare.

fig.title: Planet notes, this month
lines: Venus: a morning star, rises before the Sun
Mars: too close to the Sun to observe

q: Approaching the Tuamotus from the Marquesas at dusk, you most want your distance off the atolls. Which star do you take first?
why: A position line runs at 90° to the bearing: Canopus at 214° gives a line along the chain, 124°–304°, so your distance off it.

fig.title: Dusk, 11 May, 30 M from the Tuamotus

q: Your three stars were spread about 120° apart and their lines give this small cocked hat. Where do you put the fix?
a: In the middle of the triangle
o: At the corner nearest the DR
Outside the triangle, towards the stars
On the line of the brightest star
why: With the bodies spread round the horizon, the true position most likely lies inside a small hat: take its centre.

q: At dawn you chose two stars on almost opposite bearings, and their lines lie parallel, 3 miles apart. What does that tell you?
a: You are near the line midway between them
o: You are on the line of the brighter star
Nothing — parallel lines are of no use
You are 3 M beyond the farther line
why: A constant error (dip, index error) moves the two lines opposite ways; the mean line between them is free of it.

q: Bound from Fiji to Tonga, you have just crossed the 180th meridian eastbound. You take Rigil Kent at dusk and work it from the DR. What do you plot?
You plan dawn stars on the way from the Marquesas to Tahiti. When do you come on deck?
a: Before 0516, to find the stars in the dark
o: After 0602, once the horizon is bright
why: Find the stars and preset the sextant while it is still dark; shoot as the horizon sharpens, between nautical and civil twilight.

q: At 0300 you took three stars by the light of a nearly full Moon and plotted them. Which line do you distrust?
a: Hamal's — it bore under the Moon
o: Dubhe's — it was the lowest of the three
None — moonlight gives a true horizon
why: The horizon under the Moon's glitter may be false; the line of the star taken beneath it is the one to doubt and re-shoot at dawn.

q: After two cloudy days your DR may be 40 miles out. How far from your preset Hc may Sirius appear when you look for it?
a: Up to about 40′ — sweep a little up and down
o: Up to about 4′ — it will be in the eyepiece
Up to about 4° — use the star finder instead
Not at all — a DR error does not change Hc
why: 1′ of altitude is 1 M of distance: a 40 M error in the DR can put the star up to 40′ off the preset Hc, and its Zn a little out too.

fig.title: After two cloudy days
lines: DR uncertain by up to 40 M

q: Four dusk stars from one AP: three lines meet within a mile, but Regulus comes out like this. What most likely went wrong?
a: Its sextant reading was 1° out — add 1° and rework
o: Its time was a minute out — rework the GHA
It was the wrong star — leave it out
Refraction was left out — add it to Hs
why: 58.7′ away, against 1.3′ towards that fits the other three, is 60′: Hs was read or written 1° low.

q: Leaving the Bay of Islands for Tonga, you list the dusk stars. Which two would give almost the same position line?
why: Two stars on almost the same bearing give almost the same line; keep the higher one and spend the time on another bearing.

q: At 0100 LMT a brilliant, steady white light stands high in the sky, and your crew calls it Venus. Which planet is it?
a: Jupiter — Venus is never far from the Sun
o: Venus — it is the brightest planet
Mars — it is brightest at midnight
Saturn — it is the slowest planet
why: Venus is never more than about 47° from the Sun, so it is never high in the middle of the night; a brilliant white planet there is Jupiter.

fig.title: 15 Jan, 20°N 60°W, 0100 LMT
lines: The Sun set seven hours ago

q: Cloud leaves you only two stars, and their lines cut at 30°. If one line is a mile out, how far can that move the fix?
a: About 2.0 M along the other line
o: About 1.0 M along the other line
About 0.5 M along the other line
About 1.2 M along the other line
why: Moving one line 1 M shifts the cut 1 / sin 30° = 2 M along the other line; at a 90° cut it would be only 1 M.

fig.title: Two-star fix
lines: Each line good to about 1 M

q: After two days of cloud your star intercepts are all about 30 miles, though the lines meet in a small hat. What do you do next?
a: Rework the sights with the fix as a new DR
o: Plot it as it is — the hat is small
Take a point halfway back to the DR
Shorten each intercept by a tenth
why: A position line is a short straight piece of a large circle; with intercepts over about 30′ the curve tells, so rework from the new position.

q: Bound from Iceland for Newfoundland, you take Kochab at dusk at 58°N and work it from the DR. What Hc and Zn do you get?
why: GHA★ = GHA Aries + SHA: LHA = 349°10.8′ + 137°18′ − 30°10′ = 96°18.8′. Kochab never sets here, so a slip still gives a believable Hc.

q: Your dusk and dawn star fixes are 11 hours apart. The dawn fix lies here against your DR. What current has set you overnight?
why: DR to fix over the 11 h is the current: 6.6 M ÷ 11 h = 0.6 kn, setting 290°, from the DR towards the fix.

q: You will reduce tonight's Jupiter and Moon sights with HO 249. Which volume do you open?
a: Vol 2 or 3, with Lat, LHA and Dec
o: Vol 1, with Lat and LHA Aries
Vol 1 for Jupiter, Vol 3 for the Moon
None — HO 249 is for stars only
why: Vol 1 holds selected stars only; Vols 2 (Lat 0°–39°) and 3 (40°–89°) take any body with Dec up to 29°, planets and the Moon included.

q: Before dawn you want a Moon sight to go with the stars. Which limb do you expect to bring down to the horizon?
a: The upper limb — the lit side faces up
o: The lower limb — the Sun is below the horizon
The lower limb — it is the one used at night
Either — a gibbous Moon is lit all round
why: The lit limb faces the Sun along the great circle to it; from a Moon high in the west that circle runs up over the zenith, so the top is lit.

fig.title: 0330, three days after full Moon
lines: The Sun rises at 0610, in the east

q: On your first night in the southern sky, you look for the Southern Cross to find Acrux and see this. Is it the Cross?
a: Probably the False Cross — find the Pointers first
o: Yes — it is the only cross in the sky
Yes — take its brightest star as Acrux
No — that shape is Orion's Belt
why: The False Cross is bigger and fainter; the real Cross is small, with two bright Pointers, Rigil Kent and Hadar, leading to it.

fig.title: Looking south at dusk
lines: A cross of four stars, mag about 2
No bright pair of stars beside it

q: Bound for Nouméa at night, your three-star fix gives this large cocked hat, with the barrier reef to the south-west. What do you do?
a: Assume the corner nearest the reef and rework
o: Take the centre and hold your course
Take the corner nearest the DR and hold on
Ignore the fix and trust the DR
why: A big hat means a bad sight or a slip: until you find it, navigate from the most dangerous corner, keep sea room, and rework or re-shoot.

q: Cloud closes in after Jupiter and Spica, whose lines cut at about 90°. How far do you trust this fix?
a: A good cut, but no check against a bad sight
o: Fully — two lines at 90° cannot be wrong
Not at all — a planet and a star do not mix
For latitude only — Spica is near the meridian
why: Two lines always meet somewhere, so a blunder in either goes unseen; use the fix with care and add a third body as soon as you can.
